marble.name: Thunder & Lightning
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Know that thunder and lightning happen during thunderstorms: lightning is a giant spark of electricity that forms in clouds, thunder is the sound the lightning makes, and we see lightning before hearing thunder because light travels faster than sound
marble.prompt: During a thunderstorm, can you explain that lightning is electricity in the clouds, thunder is its sound, and that we see the flash before the boom because light is faster than sound?

cluster.summary: Your child is discovering how weather works — learning about different types of weather, how to stay safe during storms, and understanding how weather patterns change with the seasons.

misconceptions: Thunder and lightning are separate events — thunder is the SOUND made by the lightning
Lightning comes before thunder in time — they happen together; we just SEE the flash before the sound arrives
Thunder can hurt you — it is only a sound; the danger is the lightning
Bigger/louder thunder means the lightning is more dangerous — loudness mainly reflects how close it is
Light and sound travel at the same speed
representations: Flash-then-boom timeline showing the delay between seeing and hearing
A storm at varying distances with the second-count shrinking as it nears
Storm-cloud charge-separation diagram (charge builds, then a spark jumps)
Light-vs-sound speed comparison (light arrows instant, sound arrows slow)
authoredAnswer: They happen at essentially the same instant — the lightning heats the air so fast it explodes outward and that IS the thunder. You see the flash first because light travels vastly faster than sound, so the bang takes a few seconds to reach your ears. Counting the gap tells you roughly how far away the strike is.

wrongAnswers.wrong: They happen at different times — first the lightning, then later the thunder starts.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: treats the gap as a real time-difference between two events
wrongAnswers.fix: Same-event framing — flash and bang are born together; distance just makes the sound late.

wrongAnswers.wrong: You see the flash first because light is stronger than sound.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: explains the order by intensity rather than speed
wrongAnswers.fix: A distant clap: you see it before you hear it — light is faster, not stronger.
Near strike = almost no gap; far strike = long gap. Count the seconds.
